title: Writing & Handwriting
description: From strong hands and first marks to letter formation, sentences, paragraphs and purposeful writing for real audiences. Physical skills (grip, formation) are built alongside composition (ideas, organisation, revision).

lessons.title: Magic Lines and Circles
objectives: Draw straight, curved and zigzag lines with control
Hold a crayon with a tripod grip (thumb, pointer and middle finger)
prerequisites: Can hold a crayon and make marks
explanation: Before we write letters, we practise the lines that letters are made of. Every letter is built from straight lines, curves and circles.
A good grip is like a little bird beak: your thumb and pointer finger pinch the pencil, and your middle finger is the cushion underneath. Hold it gently, not too tight.
Start at the top and go down. Circles for letters like o go round anticlockwise, the same way the hands of a clock go backwards.

vocabulary.meaning: how you hold your pencil
a long thin mark
a bending line, like a rainbow
a line that goes up and down in sharp points

examples: Straight down lines make rain falling from a cloud.
Round and round circles make bubbles, balls and the letter o.

story.title: The Rain and the Rainbow
story.text: Rangi the chameleon wanted to draw a rainy day. "Start at the top and go down," said Rangi, drawing rain lines: down, down, down. Then the sun came out. Rangi drew a big curve across the sky — a rainbow! "Lines and curves," Rangi smiled, "are the secret pieces of every letter."

lessons.title: My Name Is Special
objectives: Recognise their own written name
Write their first name with a capital letter first
explanation: Your name is a special word. When we write a name, the first letter is a capital (a big letter) and the rest are small letters.
Each letter has a starting point. Most letters start at the top. For a name like Ivaan: I is a straight line down; v goes down-up; a is a round curve then a line; n is down, up and over.
Practise by tracing first, then copying, then writing from memory. Every time you write your name, your hand remembers a little more.

vocabulary.meaning: a big letter used at the start of names
the usual letters we write most of the time
draw over lines that are already there

examples: Ivaan starts with a capital I.
Mumbai, Asha and Tara all start with capital letters because they are names.

story.title: The Name on the Door
story.text: Momo the bear made a sign for the new treehouse. "Whose house is this?" asked Kiko. "It needs a name!" Momo wrote M — a big capital — then o, m, o. "MOMO'S HOUSE," read Kiko. Now everyone knew whose treehouse it was.

lessons.title: Curly Caterpillar Letters
objectives: Form c, a, d, o, g, q correctly starting at the "c" curve
Write letters with consistent size on a line
explanation: Some letters start with the same move: a curly caterpillar "c" shape. Start at the top right, curl round to the left and come back. That makes c.
For a, d, g, o and q, start with the same curl, then add something: a closes the circle and adds a short line; d adds a tall line; g adds a tail that hangs below the line.
Letters sit on the line like people sit on a bench. Tall letters (d, l) reach up; tail letters (g, q, y) hang down below the line.

vocabulary.meaning: the way you move your pencil to make a letter
turning the opposite way to clock hands
the line letters sit on

examples: c + short stick = a.
c + tall stick = d.

story.title: Callie the Caterpillar
story.text: Callie the caterpillar loved curling up. When she curled, she made a c. When she curled and held a stick, she was an a. When she curled and climbed a tall tree, she was a d! "I'm a whole letter family," she giggled.

lessons.title: Say It, Write It, Check It
objectives: Write a simple sentence with a capital letter, spaces and a full stop
Say a sentence aloud before writing it
prerequisites: Can write CVC words using sounds
explanation: A sentence is a group of words that makes complete sense: "The cat sat on the mat." It starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
Good writers say their sentence out loud first, then count the words on their fingers. That way they don't forget words.
Leave a finger space between words so readers can tell where each word ends. Then read it back to check: does it make sense?

vocabulary.meaning: words that make a complete idea
the dot at the end of a sentence
the gap between words
read again to find mistakes

examples: "I can run." — 3 words, a capital I, a full stop.
"A big dog ran to the park." — 7 words.

story.title: The Words That Squashed Together
story.text: Kiko wrote: "igotabigred ball". Nobody could read it! Olu said, "Let's say it first: I got a big red ball. Six words. Now put a finger space between each word, a capital I, and a full stop." Kiko wrote: "I got a big red ball." Everyone could read it now.

activities.prompt: Which is a correct sentence?

lessons.title: My Day Recount
objectives: Write a recount with an opening, events in order and an ending
Use time words to show order
explanation: A recount tells about something that really happened. It answers: Who? Where? When? What happened? The opening sets the scene: "On Sunday, I went to the beach with my family."
Events go in time order. Time words help the reader follow: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Recounts are written in the past tense because the events already happened: went, saw, played, ate. End with a feeling or thought: "It was the best day ever because…"

vocabulary.meaning: writing that retells real events in order
words that show when things happened
verbs that show something already happened

examples: First, we built a sandcastle. Next, a wave knocked it down.
Finally, we ate ice cream and walked home.

story.title: Zuri's Jumbled Diary
story.text: Zuri wrote: "We ate lunch. Finally we woke up. Then we went to the zoo." Her friends were confused. Zuri rewrote it: "First, we woke up early. Then we went to the zoo. After that, we ate lunch. Finally, we went home tired and happy." Now it made sense.

activities.prompt: Put the recount in order
Which is in the past tense?
options: I will go to the park.

activities.prompt: Match the present to the past
A recount tells about something that really happened.

thinking: Why does the order matter in a recount?
How is a recount different from a made-up story?
speaking: Tell someone about your weekend using at least four time words, then write it down.

units.summary: Conjunctions join ideas into longer, richer sentences.
objectives: Join two ideas using and, but, so or because
Explain the difference in meaning between the conjunctions

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: And, But, Because
objectives: Join two ideas using and, but, so or because
Explain the difference in meaning between the conjunctions
prerequisites: Writes simple sentences with correct punctuation
explanation: Conjunctions are joining words. "And" adds another idea: I like apples and I like mangoes. "But" shows a contrast: I like apples but I don't like pears.
"Because" gives a reason: I took an umbrella because it was raining. "So" gives a result: It was raining, so I took an umbrella.
Joining ideas makes writing flow and shows how ideas are connected — not just a list of short sentences.

vocabulary.meaning: a word that joins words or ideas
showing a difference
why something happens
what happens because of something

examples: The dog was hungry, so it barked.
I wanted to play outside, but it was dark.

story.title: The Choppy Robot
story.text: Bolt spoke in tiny sentences. "I went out. It rained. I got wet. I was sad." Rangi taught Bolt joining words. Bolt tried: "I went out, but it rained, so I got wet. I was sad because my circuits were dripping!" Everyone laughed — now Bolt sounded like a storyteller.

activities.prompt: "I wore a coat ___ it was cold."
"I like football ___ I don't like cricket."
Match the conjunction to its job
"So" tells us a result.

thinking: Do "because" and "so" mean the same thing? Try swapping them in a sentence.
Can too many "and"s make writing worse? Why?
speaking: Make three sentences about your day: one with "but", one with "because" and one with "so". Say them aloud.

lessons.title: Climbing the Story Mountain
objectives: Plan a story using a story mountain
Write a story in paragraphs with a clear problem and resolution
prerequisites: Writes sentences in order using conjunctions
explanation: Many stories follow a "story mountain": an opening (meet the characters and setting), a build-up (something starts to happen), a problem (the top of the mountain), a resolution (how it is solved) and an ending.
Planning first saves time. Jot notes or quick pictures for each part before writing sentences.
Use a new paragraph for each part of the mountain, or when time, place or speaker changes. Paragraphs help readers follow the journey.

vocabulary.meaning: the events of a story
where and when a story happens
how the problem is solved
a group of sentences about one idea or moment

examples: Opening: Meera lived by the sea. Problem: a storm trapped a baby turtle. Resolution: Meera built a channel to the waves.
A new paragraph starts when the scene moves from the beach to Meera's house.

story.title: The Story That Never Ended
story.text: Kiko wrote a story where a dragon found a cave, then a river, then a forest, then another cave… and nothing ever happened. "Where's the problem?" asked Nova. Kiko added: the dragon lost its fire. The search for its fire became the adventure — and finally the story had a top of the mountain.

activities.prompt: Put the story mountain in order
Where do we meet the characters and setting?

lessons.title: ARMS and CUPS
objectives: Revise writing by adding, removing, moving or replacing words
Edit for capitals, punctuation and spelling
explanation: Writers rarely get it right first time. Revising improves the ideas: ARMS — Add details, Remove repetition, Move sentences to a better place, Substitute stronger words.
Editing fixes the surface: CUPS — Capitals, Usage (does the grammar sound right?), Punctuation, Spelling.
Reading your work aloud is the best trick. Your ears catch mistakes your eyes skip.

vocabulary.meaning: change writing to make the ideas better
correct mistakes in spelling, punctuation and grammar
an early version of writing
comments to help improve work

examples: Before: "The dog was nice." After revising: "The scruffy dog wagged its tail and licked my hand."
Editing: "i went to delhi" → "I went to Delhi."

story.title: The Messy First Draft
story.text: Rangi showed Olu a first draft full of crossings-out. "It's ruined!" said Rangi. Olu smiled and opened a famous writer's notebook — it was covered in crossings-out too! "Messy drafts are where good writing comes from," said Olu.

activities.prompt: Which is editing (CUPS), not revising?

lessons.title: Build an Argument
objectives: Write a persuasive text with a clear claim, reasons and evidence
Address a counter-argument
explanation: Persuasive writing tries to convince the reader. Start with a clear claim: "Our school should have a vegetable garden." Then give reasons, each in its own paragraph, supported by evidence such as facts, examples or expert views.
Strong arguments answer the other side. A counter-argument paragraph says: "Some people think it costs too much. However…" This shows you have thought carefully.
Persuasive language includes modal verbs (should, must, could), rhetorical questions ("Wouldn't you like fresh food?"), and a confident conclusion that restates the claim.

vocabulary.meaning: the main point you are arguing
facts or examples that support a reason
the opposing view
a word like should, must, could showing how certain or necessary something is

examples: Reason: gardens teach science. Evidence: students can observe plant life cycles first-hand.
Counter-argument: "Some say it takes too much time. However, it could replace one lesson a week."

story.title: The Great Playground Letter
story.text: Zuri's class wanted a new playground bench. Their first letter said, "We want a bench. Please." Nothing happened. Their second letter gave reasons (grandparents waiting at pick-up had nowhere to sit), evidence (a count of 14 people standing each day), and answered cost worries. The bench arrived a month later.

Which is evidence?

activities.prompt: Which is a rhetorical question?

activities.prompt: Addressing the other side can make your argument stronger.

lessons.title: Explaining How and Why
objectives: Write a clear explanation of a process using cause-and-effect language
Use diagrams and technical vocabulary to support writing
prerequisites: Writes in paragraphs and uses conjunctions
explanation: An explanation tells how or why something happens — like how rain forms or why we have seasons. It begins with a general statement introducing the topic.
Then it explains the process in a logical sequence, using cause-and-effect connectives: because, therefore, as a result, consequently, this causes.
Technical words should be used precisely and explained when needed. Diagrams with labels make complex processes much clearer.

vocabulary.meaning: a series of steps that lead to a result
words that link sentences and paragraphs
specialist words for a subject
as a result

examples: "The Sun heats water in oceans. As a result, it evaporates and rises as water vapour."
"When the vapour cools, it condenses into tiny droplets, which form clouds."

story.title: Why Is the Sky Dark at Night?
story.text: Bolt was asked, "Why is it dark at night?" Bolt answered, "Because it is night." Nobody was satisfied. Bolt tried again: "The Earth spins. As a result, our side faces away from the Sun for part of each day, so less sunlight reaches us." Now it was an explanation.

activities.prompt: An explanation usually starts with…
options: a general statement about the topic

activities.prompt: Which connective shows cause and effect?
Order the water cycle explanation
Diagrams can help explain a process.

speaking: Explain how a bicycle's brakes stop it, using at least two cause-and-effect connectives.

lessons.title: Writing a Strong Thesis
objectives: Write an arguable, specific thesis statement
Structure analytical paragraphs that develop the thesis
prerequisites: Writes persuasive and explanatory texts in paragraphs
explanation: A thesis is the central claim of an essay. A strong thesis is arguable (someone could disagree), specific (not vague), and gives a sense of the essay's direction.

Weak: "Social media has good and bad effects." Strong: "Although social media connects teenagers to wider communities, its design rewards constant comparison, which harms self-esteem more than it helps belonging."
Each body paragraph advances the thesis: a topic sentence (the paragraph's claim), evidence, analysis (why the evidence matters), and a link back to the thesis.

vocabulary.meaning: an essay's central arguable claim
a sentence stating a paragraph's main point
explaining how evidence supports a claim
the logical path through an essay

examples: Topic sentence: "The novel's setting mirrors the narrator's isolation."
Analysis: "By placing the house miles from any village, the author makes loneliness physical, not just emotional."

story.title: The Essay That Said Nothing
story.text: A student's essay concluded: "In conclusion, there are many views on homework." Her teacher wrote: "What is YOUR view?" She rewrote her thesis: "Homework in primary school should be replaced by reading time, because evidence links reading volume to achievement more strongly than set tasks." Suddenly the essay had a spine.

activities.prompt: Which is the strongest thesis?
options: There are many opinions about climate.
Cities should prioritise tree planting over new car parks because shade reduces heat-related illness.

activities.prompt: Order a body paragraph
A thesis should be something no one could disagree with.

options: why the evidence supports the claim

thinking: Can a thesis change as you write? Should it?
What makes analysis different from summary?
speaking: Present your thesis to someone and ask them to argue against it; then refine it.

lessons.title: Using Sources Honestly
objectives: Evaluate sources for reliability
Quote, paraphrase and cite sources correctly
explanation: Not all sources are equally reliable. Check: Currency (how recent?), Relevance (does it answer my question?), Authority (who wrote it and are they qualified?), Accuracy (is it supported by evidence?), Purpose (inform, sell, persuade?).
You can use a source by quoting (exact words in quotation marks), paraphrasing (its idea in your own words and structure), or summarising (the main point briefly). All three need a citation.
Plagiarism means presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. Citing sources is honest, lets readers check your evidence, and shows the research behind your thinking.

examples: Quote: According to the WHO, "physical activity reduces the risk of heart disease."
Paraphrase: Regular exercise lowers the chance of heart disease (World Health Organization).

story.title: The Copied Paragraph
story.text: Arjun pasted a paragraph from a website into his report and changed three words. His teacher found the original in seconds. Arjun rewrote it: he read the source, closed the tab, explained the idea in his own words, and added the citation. His teacher said it was the best paragraph in the report — because it was really his.
